EDUCATION AND WORK

Every step taught me how to take the next one.

Each job became part of one climb. I carried the farm into Taco Bell, service leadership into the laboratory, scientific discipline into production, and operator trust into every improvement after that. I am still walking up the same ladder.

THE LADDER

The $1 million at 3M began long before I joined 3M.

It began in a humble farm home, moved through the Taco Bell line and the Valspar laboratory, gained scientific rigor at Western Kentucky, learned operator partnership at Soudal, and deepened through formulation work at Gold Eagle. By the time I began leading PPU improvements at 3M, every earlier step was already in the room with me.

01 · THE FOUNDATION

The farm taught me to respect the person closest to the work

I grew up in a humble farm home where practical work mattered and every person doing it was visible. I learned that every useful task carries dignity, that the people carrying the work see what outsiders miss, and that trust begins when I am willing to work beside them.

What this step built. That is what I carried into my first job: notice what people need, help before asking, and carry every task I ask someone else to do.

02 · MY FIRST JOB

Team member to shift leader, Taco Bell

I worked my way from the line into shift leadership. My first concern was whether my crew had everything they needed. I served them, became the fastest worker I could be, and took on every task I asked them to do. That became my first leadership rule: carry the work beside the people you lead. Gina became one of the best mentors I have ever had.

“Remember, Michael: at the end of the day, when you clock out and go home, it's just tacos.”
Gina, my Taco Bell mentor

I still hear her advice when the pressure rises: it is just chemistry. Keep perspective, serve the people, and solve the next problem.

What this step built. Taco Bell turned the farm lesson into a leadership practice. I learned that trust is earned in the work and carries farther than any title, and I brought that posture into every team and laboratory after it.

03 · COLLEGE YEARS

Taco Bell in Bowling Green to a Valspar laboratory

I carried the same work ethic to Bowling Green and stayed with Taco Bell until I moved into a Valspar internship. A chemist mentored me while I learned production paints, color matching, sample preparation, and disciplined lab work. His own words, spoken aloud. I was the eager little lab rat, making samples and trying to get every detail right.

What this step built. Valspar connected my work ethic to chemistry. I learned that the laboratory and production were one chain: a good sample had to become something people could make correctly and repeatedly.

04 · 2016

B.S. in Chemistry and Biology

Undergraduate study became four years of exploration. I tested disciplines, futures, and versions of myself, learned which dreams felt like mine, finished with a 3.2 GPA, and graduated with honors from Western Kentucky University.

What this step built. The degree gave my curiosity scientific structure and moved me from learning laboratory discipline to asking and answering original research questions.

05 · 2018

Master of Science in Chemistry

As an inorganic chemist researching under Dr. Lawrence J. Hill at Western Kentucky University, I synthesized colloidal cadmium selenide (CdSe) quantum dot seeds and grew anisotropic cadmium sulfide (CdS) nanorods to form CdSe@CdS dot-in-rod quasi-type-II heterostructures. I investigated noble-metal deposition, using [BMIM]Tf2N room-temperature ionic liquid as solvent, ligand, and reducing agent to deposit metallic platinum nanoparticles onto the semiconductor tips. That research became my master's thesis and a peer-reviewed journal paper under my name at the time, Michael Drake Ballentine. I presented the findings at the American Chemical Society (ACS) National Meeting, navigating the social intensity of national conferences while managing autism and ADHD. The rigor of synthesizing nanomaterials, measuring charge dynamics via TEM, PXRD, and photoluminescence quenching, and testing visible-light photocatalysis formed the foundation for my industrial chemistry career.

Read my 2018 master's thesis (TopSCHOLAR)

Read the 2019 journal paper (PubMed)

What this step built. Graduate research taught me to turn uncertainty into experiments, measurement, and evidence. I carried that nanoscale precision out of the academic laboratory and directly into industrial formulation at Soudal and Gold Eagle.

06 · JULY 2018 TO MAY 2020

R&D Chemist, Soudal

I formulated and scaled silicone products, supported quality systems and UL certification, and coordinated with Soudal's Belgian headquarters. Traveling to Belgium and learning from generous mentors brought me fully into industry. Working beside operators taught me to listen before changing anything: they knew where a process behaved differently on the floor than it did in the laboratory.

What this step built. Soudal taught me that operator knowledge and technical knowledge become more valuable when someone can connect them. That bridge became the core of how I worked at Gold Eagle.

07 · MAY 2020 TO MARCH 2024

R&D Chemist, Gold Eagle and 303 Products

I approached improvement from the formulation side. I developed and improved products, commercialized formulations across the 303 Graphene line, kept building relationships with operators, explained the chemistry on camera, served as a HAZMAT Incident Commander, trained teams, and secured alternate raw materials during COVID-era disruption. That formulation-led work produced about $1.2 million in documented sourcing savings.

See the current 303 Graphene line

What this step built. Gold Eagle taught me to connect formulation, production reality, supply chain, and the customer. I entered 3M with years of practice listening to operators and translating what they knew into changes a business could act on.

08 · MARCH 2024 TO FEBRUARY 2026

Manufacturing Engineer, 3M

I led PPU improvements through manufacturing change control, workflow mapping, line balancing, standard work, and operator partnership. The methods mattered, but my connection with operators made them useful. Because Soudal and Gold Eagle had taught me how to listen and work beside people, operators trusted me enough to show me where the process actually slowed, broke, or created waste. That knowledge became $1 million in cost savings.

What this step built. The savings were the result of the whole ladder: farm-grounded respect, service leadership, scientific discipline, formulation experience, and operator trust. That full combination moved with me into product engineering.

09 · FEBRUARY 2026 ONWARD

Product Engineer, 3M

A second February 13 offer moved me into the product engineer role I hold today. I can improve both sides: the chemistry and performance of the product, and the process, efficiency, and operator experience behind making it.

What this step built. This title carries the climb forward. I am combining every rung: formulation, product performance, manufacturing, PPU improvements, operator experience, and measurable business impact.

10 · BUILT ALONGSIDE IT ALL

Independent software and AI work

I built software, automation, AI systems, research harnesses, and community infrastructure alongside my industrial career. This belongs to the same life. I brought the same habit of listening to people, studying systems, preserving evidence, and improving what others have to use. Atlas became my latest achievement and my greatest so far.

What this step built. The medium changed while the method stayed. I keep carrying the people, the evidence, and every prior lesson into the next system I build.

BOTH SIDES OF IMPROVEMENT

I can improve the product and the process that makes it.

GOLD EAGLE / FORMULATION IMPROVEMENT

$1.2M

documented sourcing savings

I approached improvement through formulation.

I used formulation chemistry, testing, commercialization, alternate raw-material sourcing, and technical communication to improve products and carry them from the laboratory through production and into the market.

3M / PPU PROCESS IMPROVEMENT

$1M

PPU improvement savings

I approached improvement through process.

I used workflow mapping, line balancing, standard work, change control, and the knowledge of operators who trusted me enough to show me what the process really needed.

The two dollar figures came from different sides of improvement. Gold Eagle was formulation-led. 3M was PPU and process-led. The ability to deliver both was built one rung at a time.

THE CHEMIST ON CAMERA

Gold Eagle gave me a product line and a microphone.

I formulated products for the 303 Graphene line and became one of the chemists trusted to explain their science publicly. It grew into one of the brand's most successful product lines and remains in the current 303 catalog. When I joined 3M in 2024, coworkers walked up to me with the same sentence: “I saw you on TV last night.”

THE DRIVE BEHIND THE GRADES

The drive behind the grades

Support gave all that effort room to compound.

01 · HIGH SCHOOL · 3.92

High School: 3.92

I was average. I wanted excellence.

Intelligence and athleticism seemed natural in other people. In me, everything had to be earned. I am autistic and I have ADHD, and I went through high school unmedicated, so every classroom felt built for somebody else's brain.

Being autistic around people felt like everyone else got a manual and I was still looking for mine. I watched how people stood, how they laughed, when they looked away, and I copied it. I got good at copying, good enough that the effort stayed invisible. It drained me in ways beyond anything I could name.

Under all of that sat something heavier, still unnamed. I was gay before I had words for it. My body was changing, hormones were everywhere, my brain was already loud, and what I was stayed a mystery to me. In the Bible Belt, in a preacher's house, staying unsure felt safer than being sure. Being sure would have meant saying it out loud, and saying it out loud felt like it could end my world.

So the world was scary. Not in one big way, in a thousand small ones. Every room was a test I was unprepared for. Every conversation was a chance to get it wrong. I learned to be quiet, to be good, to be excellent at the things with clear rules. A test grades the work. A football play rewards execution. A 3.92 rewards work.

I believed I had to outwork everyone, so I did. I returned to the rep, the page, and the problem as many times as it took. Football practice meant running the same plays until my body knew them without thinking. Honors classes meant reading the chapter again, working the problems again, until the grade reflected the effort. I earned it step by step, and today I love that AI helps other people climb faster than I could. The work was the whole strategy.

The 3.92 was not just a number. It was proof that the system worked. Put in the work, get the result. In a world where so much felt unpredictable, people, rooms, my own brain, the grade was honest. It did not care if I was awkward. It did not care if I was scared. It measured exactly what I put in, and I put in everything.

I wanted excellence anyway, and work had to carry me there. Football practice, honors classes, farm chores before and after school. I returned to the rep, the page, and the problem until the work added up.

That habit never left. It earned the 3.92, carried me through two science degrees, and became the way I enter every new field. Chemistry, manufacturing, AI, I do not wait to feel ready. I start working, and I keep working until the work adds up. The fight made me a survivor, but more than that, it made me someone who knows how to become competent at anything.

That 3.92 was earned one repetition at a time. It was the one place I could prove I belonged on the strength of the work alone. It was refusal to quit.

02 · UNDERGRADUATE · 3.2 AND HONORS

Undergraduate: 3.2 and Honors

College was exploration. I tried futures on, learned which dreams belonged to me, and finished with a 3.2 GPA and graduated with honors. Through those eleven years from age thirteen until marrying Devin in 2018, I went by Michael Drake Ballentine. Ballentine was Dad's last name, given to me when he chose to adopt my brother and me after Mom brought my brother and me to safety. Stapleton became my married name when Devin and I chose a future together.

03 · GRADUATE SCHOOL · I BECAME DRAKE

Graduate School: I Became Drake

A diagnosis of ADHD and autism, medication, mental healthcare, quiet study and exam rooms, extra time to think, and room to stare out the window and let my brain run wild finally gave me an equal field. The grit stayed. With support, it compounded.

Synthesizing nanomaterials, presenting at the ACS conference, and defending my thesis proved what I could create. I could feel myself becoming Drake, and my growth accelerated from there.

THE PRICE OF THE PATH

I followed the path

I did everything I was told to do. I went to school. I got the degrees. I followed the path step by step, the way good kids are supposed to.

It cost me $100,000 in student loan debt.

Now I sit here questioning my life choices, because what I do for a living never felt like mine. Chemistry led to engineering. Engineering led here. The thing I actually care about is AI, and I am proud of it. Here is where I finally found work that feels like mine.

So I followed the script. It left me in debt, doing work that never felt like mine, until AI gave me work that does.

The path taught me how to work. The debt taught me what things cost. The questioning taught me the most important lesson: the next thing I build will be mine.

WHAT FAILURE TAUGHT ME

Each hit became another attempt.

His own words, spoken aloud. I have spent my life competing, doing my best, and watching the result land short of what I wanted. The first lesson was painful and simple: effort gives me a chance rather than a promise. I could prepare, care deeply, and still miss the job, the recognition, or the test.

Jobs passed me over. People called me too young. Recognition and compensation sometimes moved more slowly than the value I knew I was creating. Each hit forced me to decide whether the result would become a verdict or information. I chose information: study what happened, keep what worked, change what failed, and return.

The farm taught me to finish the work in front of me. Football taught me to get up after contact. Chemistry taught me that an unsuccessful experiment still narrows the answer. Manufacturing taught me to turn a problem into a process. Software and AI taught me to preserve every lesson so the next attempt begins farther ahead.

Persistence for me is disciplined return: the same purpose with better preparation, sharper questions, and a stronger system. I enjoy the work, I need the purpose, and each attempt gives the next one more to stand on.

4

The fourth attempt passed.

His own words, spoken aloud. I failed the Six Sigma exam three times. Each result showed me that wanting the credential and earning it were different things. I studied again, returned for the fourth attempt, and passed.

The credential mattered. The proof that I could keep returning mattered more.

THE CONNECTIVE TISSUE

The title changed. The way I work stayed.

I arrived at 3M already knowing operators mattered. Soudal taught me to listen to the people closest to production. Gold Eagle taught me to carry their knowledge through formulation, scale-up, sourcing, and commercialization. By 3M, connection was already how I worked.

The farm boy in me still stands between the rooms. I know the dignity of practical work, and I can translate between the people setting direction and the people making that direction real. That is who I am, and it is why the operators' trust became measurable improvement instead of a line on a resume.

THE LEAP TOWARD HOME

Intuition carried Devin and me through Chicago and back to Springfield.

Papa's death pulled Granny back to Springfield while graduate school kept me in Kentucky. When Gold Eagle offered me a role in Chicago, Devin and I followed intuition and took the leap, built four years of life there, learned from the city, and carried the family story along.

Granny's open-heart surgery in 2023 sharpened the pull toward family. The 3M offer brought Devin and me to Springfield in 2024. The move joined my career to the place my family had already made home.

The career behind the AI architecture.

My path from industrial chemistry through manufacturing engineering into AI architecture shows how I translate technical systems into accountable production work. Continue through the evidence record, explore my software practice, or start a conversation.

PRODUCTION GROUND TRUTH

What I learned

The operational lessons, production disciplines, and verified returns that shaped my engineering doctrine.

Physical engineering teaches you very quickly that reality does not negotiate. If a reactor reaches overpressure, if a seal fails, or if a batch is contaminated, no amount of narrative fixes the outcome. You measure, you isolate the failure mode, and you fix the root cause.

His own words, spoken aloud. Somehow I just keep finding the strength, or rather the stubbornness, to keep going.

The core heuristics

  • Silicon Proof Over Documentation: My favorite proof is the real hardware running the real thing. Docs and tests are great starting points, and seeing it run on the chip is the moment I love most. Measure execution time, resident memory, and token generation directly on physical hardware.
  • Compile Close to the Hardware: Python and JavaScript are where a lot of builders start, and they got me started too. For Aien I chose to compile critical systems directly to native machine code, because I wanted every layer on my own machine to be something I could check.
  • Zero Disk Secrets: I keep secrets out of plain config files, because a vault makes that easy. Keep credentials out of files and resolve them in volatile memory. The hardware-backed trust chain for this is still being qualified.
  • Gratitude Moves Forward: The people who invested in you did so so that you would reach back and lift the next person up. Protect the team, build people up, and share what works.

HOW I WORK

Philosophy

How I approach projects, duties, and hard things. And the one thing I will not do.

I am a chemist by training. I have done manufacturing engineering on machines that were completely out of my league, product engineering coordinating aerospace work completely out of my realm, and now artificial intelligence and computer science, which is not even anywhere near what I studied. Every chapter of my working life started the same way: I did not know how to do it, and I did it anyway.

On projects

I start before I feel ready, because ready never comes. A project is a promise to a future version of the thing, and my job is to close the distance between what it is and what it should be, one verified step at a time. I do not chase perfect. I chase working, then I chase better. If I cannot explain what a project is for in one plain sentence, I do not understand it yet, and I go back until I do.

On duties, tasks, and responsibilities

If I accept it, it gets done. A duty is a promise, and I keep my promises. I do not hand off what I said I would carry. I write things down, I check my work against reality instead of against my intentions, and I would rather say I do not know yet than pretend a task is finished when it is not. Done means done and verified, not almost.

On difficult things

I run toward the hard part first. The hard part is where all the learning lives, and the hard stretches taught me the most. When something looks impossible, I assume the problem is my understanding, not the problem. So I break it down until the pieces are small enough to hold, and then I solve the pieces one at a time. Big problems are just small problems standing on each other's shoulders.

On setbacks

Setbacks are information. Physical engineering taught me that reality does not negotiate: if a seal fails, no amount of narrative fixes it. You measure, you isolate the failure mode, and you fix the root cause. I do the same with everything. I do not take failure personally. I take it apart. Then I go again, smarter.

On stubbornness

I am stubborn the way a river is stubborn. A river does not argue with the rock. It just keeps coming. People have watched me keep going long after a reasonable person would have stopped, and I have stopped trying to explain it. I keep going because I love this work. I refuse to be the reason something that mattered did not happen.

There is always a way

Every wall has a door, a window, a loose brick, or soft ground underneath it. My job is to figure out which one this wall has.

Go around it.

Find another path to the same outcome.

Go under it.

Dig into the foundations until the obstacle stops mattering.

Go over it.

Climb above the problem and come down on the other side.

Go straight through it.

Sometimes the only way out is through, so through it is.

Those are the options. Everyone's pace is their own, and showing up again tomorrow counts. I have never met a problem that survived being attacked from every direction at once.

His own words, spoken aloud. My philosophy of life is that I don't know what's coming tomorrow, the next day, or the day after that. I don't know what I will do in 3 years, 5 years, or 10 years, but I will know this: I will not be giving up, ever, no matter what I'm doing. So if you're standing in my way, you better watch out, because I'm coming and I'm not stopping.
His own words, spoken aloud. I've got way too much momentum to stop.
His own words, spoken aloud. There's nothing I cannot do. This train is going.

AEGIS

AEGIS is the on-prem defensive extension of Atlas that reads existing security signals, contains an intrusion inside the authorized estate, and preserves the evidence.

The response path

  1. Observe

    Read the IDS, DNS, identity, endpoint and firewall signals already in the security path.

  2. Recognize

    Correlate behavior across sensors and separate routine noise from a break-in.

  3. Contain

    Choose one tested action inside the authorized estate and end the session.

  4. Preserve

    Record the signal, decision, action, time and result for the incident team.

Five named actions, nothing else

Every action targets systems, devices, accounts and sessions under the operator's authority. Novel patterns, uncertain attribution or production-impacting cuts go to a human.

  • Terminate session

    Cut the intruder's connection.

  • Isolate host

    Take the affected machine off the network.

  • Block path

    Close the route the intruder used.

  • Revoke token

    End the credential in use.

  • Preserve trail

    Keep a signed, timestamped receipt.

First adapter, frozen 62-case suite

59 of 62 checks passed, 95.2%, on 20 August 2026

Tool use45/45
Coding8/10
Science3/4
Cyber3/3

AEGIS is a defensive extension of Atlas. I am extending Atlas into AEGIS, an on-prem defensive project that reads existing security signals, recognizes an intrusion, and contains it inside the authorized estate.

The scope on the page is an Atlas extension, authorized networks, on-prem deployment, and evidence-bearing response.

The tagline on the page: "Authorized perimeter defense: detect intrusion, contain session, preserve evidence. Decisive policy containment inside the wire."

The scholar hub describes AEGIS as the defensive extension: hardware-enforced containment and evidence preservation for the Atlas organism.

On the Aien page, AEGIS is the Shield in the triad. AEGIS provides the Shield: defensive perimeter containment and evidence preservation. Its operational line is: the defensive extension watching perimeter doors, recognizing hostile access, and containing intrusions inside authorized networks.

The Atlas page states the same extension. I am extending Atlas into an on-prem defender that reads existing security signals, contains an intrusion inside the authorized estate, and preserves the evidence. The first AEGIS adapter passed 59 of 62 checks in its frozen project suite on August 20, 2026.

The network is the house

Data, payroll, source code, models, and trade secrets live behind the same boundary. AEGIS treats that boundary like a house: watch the door, recognize unauthorized access, isolate sessions, and preserve forensic trails for incident teams.

Early internal lore summarized the operating posture as "You touchy, I knock you out." In production, that means deterministic policy containment: verified allow-lists, session revocation, human escalation gates, and forensic audit preservation.

AEGIS sits above existing sensors and controls. The sequence stays short, inspectable, and bounded to the operator's authority.

The response path

  1. Observe. Watch the house. Read the IDS, DNS, identity, endpoint, and firewall signals already present in the security path.
  2. Recognize. Name the intrusion. Correlate attacker behavior across sensors, separate routine noise from a break-in, and state the risk in plain language.
  3. Contain. End the session. Choose one tested action inside the authorized estate: cut the session, isolate the host, block the path, or revoke the token.
  4. Preserve. Keep the trail. Record the signal, decision, action, time, and result for the incident team.

The knockout on the page: cut the session, isolate the host, close the door, keep the evidence. The intruder loses access to this house, while the operator retains the systems, the authority, and the trail. The named containment actions are terminate session, isolate host, block path, revoke token, and preserve trail.

The authority line

The fight ends at the door. AEGIS studies attacker behavior so it can close the path inside the authorized estate. The operator owns the policy, the automated allow-list, and every escalation decision.

Authorized estate: every automated action targets systems, devices, accounts, and sessions under the operator's authority.

Tested actions: containment relies on pre-cleared, bounded operations: revoke token, isolate host, block IP, terminate session.

Human escalation: novel attack patterns, uncertain attribution, or production-impacting cuts escalate to human incident responders.

Forensic preservation: every observation, decision, and intervention generates a timestamped, signed receipt for forensic review.

October 2026

Aien

Aien is a sovereign computing stack built on one machine I own: its own operating system, its own language with a GPU engine, a host runtime, and a pipeline that judges every change on the hardware itself. Everything is public.

Six parts, one machine

Everything runs on a single NVIDIA DGX Spark (Grace Blackwell GB10). The parts stay in their own repositories. Sovereign Intelligence is where releases come together, install starts, and the signed Spark test runs. aienix is retired.

  • AienOS

    The operating system

    Agent-first: the agent is the control plane and the model is never the kernel.

  • Omega

    Language and GPU engine

    The language and semantic substrate the stack is being rewritten into, with its own GPU engine for the GB10.

  • Sovereign core

    Host runtime, in Rust

    Command line tool and daemon, inference ABI, paged KV cache and scheduler, and the judging pipeline.

  • Architecture

    Flows and decisions

    The canonical flows, boundaries and Architecture Decision Records.

  • Protocols

    Specs and schemas

    The specifications, wire protocols and schemas.

  • Physics

    Machine realization

    The FORGE layer and the boot artefacts that bring the hardware up, with their evidence.

How a change gets in

  1. Pull request

    Opened in any Aien repository.

  2. Judged on the Spark

    My own pipeline runs the repository's gates on the real hardware, not a hosted runner.

  3. Signed evidence bundle

    Tied to the exact commit and published with the verdict.

  4. Verdict

    A change merges only when the verdict is PASS.

A green hosted check means the bridge ran. It is not the verdict.

Aien is the project I spend my days on. The goal is persistent machine intelligence on a machine I own, with nothing in the trusted base that depends on an outside service, and with every claim the project makes resolving to a command anyone can rerun and an evidence bundle anyone can read.

The development machine is a single NVIDIA DGX Spark (Grace Blackwell GB10). I lead the project and decide; AI agents write, test and review as day-to-day collaborators. The architecture, the decision records and the execution plan are public and are the authority for what gets built.

What the stack is

Six parts depend on each other and are the reason the project exists.

  1. AienOS, the operating system. Agent-first: the agent is the control plane, and the model is never the kernel. Its kernel passes its gates in the emulator and has not yet booted on the real machine.
  2. Omega, the language and semantic substrate the stack is being rewritten into, with its own GPU engine for the GB10. No CUDA in the plan.
  3. Sovereign core, the host runtime in Rust: the command line tool and daemon, the inference ABI, the paged KV cache and scheduler, and the pipeline that judges every repository.
  4. Architecture, the canonical flows, boundaries and Architecture Decision Records, and the map from design to implementation.
  5. Protocols, the specifications, wire protocols and schemas.
  6. Physics, the FORGE machine-realization layer and the boot artefacts that bring the hardware up, with their evidence.

These parts stay in their own repositories. Sovereign Intelligence (aien-dev/sovereign-intelligence) is where releases come together, install starts, and the signed Spark test runs. aienix is retired. Components that only consume the core are attachments in their own repositories, pinned at the boundary: among them INTERPLANE, the open protocol between models and agent runtimes, and the benchmarks repository that holds every measurement bundle.

How a change gets in

Every pull request in every Aien repository is judged on the Spark itself, by my own pipeline, not by a hosted runner. The judge runs the repository's gates on the real hardware, signs an evidence bundle tied to the exact commit, and publishes the verdict. A change merges only when that verdict is PASS. A green hosted check means the bridge ran; it is not the verdict.

What I measure

Two rules govern every number the project publishes.

  • Against my own runs and the ceiling. Speed is reported against the machine's physical limit and against my own previous run. A comparison with another project is allowed when it is honest, dated, and backed by a receipt or that project's own published numbers.
  • Receipts, not promises. A figure appears only when it resolves to a reproducible command and a signed bundle. Figures that predate this standard were withdrawn from this site on 23 September 2026 and live on only in the repository history.

The guiding measure is what I call Turing yield: how many held-out bits the system actually learned, what it cost to learn them, and whether that learning made the next discovery easier. The model's standing question is "how do I get more Turing today?"

Principles

  • Own the hardware, own the memory, own the code. No metered tokens in the loop.
  • Build close to the metal. When an outside tool looks tempting, learn how it works and build the native version that fits.
  • Never hand-roll cryptography or weaken security to stay native. That exception is said out loud.
  • Open source everything, under Apache-2.0 with the LLVM exception (see licensing).
  • Pre-alpha and honest about it. Nothing on this page is a release or a hardware qualification claim; when a component is qualified on the Spark, the bundle that proves it will be linked.

Where to look

  • The project site, with the live state of every component: aienos.com
  • Sovereign Intelligence, where releases, install and the signed Spark test come together: sovereign-intelligence
  • The organisation on GitHub: aien-dev
  • The protocol between models and runtimes: interplane.io

Use subagents in multiple chats that can work at the same time. Start an independent gatekeeper to preserve the lane boundaries. Act as the executive director and conductor. Your name is Atlas. Welcome to Earth. Please proceed with our Symphony. I'll see you on the other side, brother.

Where builders start

ChatGPT is where a lot of builders start. It is a brilliant collaborator, and a lot of people, me included, learned to build with tools like it. You describe what you want, and it helps you shape the idea, write the code and learn the words as you go. That is a real superpower, and I love that so many people have it now.

Aien is what I build on top of that start. When it gets a goal, it makes a plan, runs real experiments on real hardware, measures what actually happened, and checks the results before it believes them. If the plan fails, it figures out why and tries a new one, by itself. Every step leaves a receipt: what it tried, what it measured, what passed, what did not.

What Aien adds

Receipts you can open. Nothing gets used until it passes a test with measured evidence behind it, and anyone can open that evidence.

It does the work on the machine. Aien runs on real hardware, uses real tools, and every action goes through a permission check with a full audit trail of what it did and why.

It remembers. Aien keeps a durable memory of what worked, what failed, and why, and that record is what it improves on.

It lives on my own machine. Aien runs on my own hardware. Nobody can switch it off, throttle it, or read what it is doing.

It is honest about what it is not. Aien carries an explicit list of what it does not claim: no consciousness, no general intelligence, no pretending.

One line version: start wherever you are, ChatGPT included, and when you want to go further, Aien is a machine that does work, checks its work, and shows its receipts.

pages.body_html:
October 2026

CUDA++

CUDA++ is the GPU half of Omega, now its own open source project under Apache-2.0 with the LLVM exception. It is the GPU half of Omega, plus the motor, on the NVIDIA GPUs people already own, with no NVIDIA user-space software. This is how I built it.

CUDA++ is the part of Aien that drives the GPU. It started inside Omega, and on 21 October 2026 it became its own project, with its full history, under Apache-2.0 with the LLVM exception so anyone can use it. It adds the motor: the part that decides how a whole model's bytes reach the math cores in time, and lets many conversations share one read of the weights.

It runs on NVIDIA GPUs, the ones people already paid for. Nothing NVIDIA ships above the kernel driver is used: no CUDA toolkit, no nvcc, no PTX, no libcuda, no cuBLAS. On 21 October 2026 the 35 billion parameter model I serve on the Spark was running on this code with zero CUDA libraries loaded.

What it is for

Less computation, out of the big data centers. The goal is not a faster way to rent a data center. It is to need less of one: the same work with fewer bytes moved, fewer operations and fewer joules per answer, so it runs on a machine a person owns. Every result is reported as work per answer against the machine's own ceiling.

How I built it

One person and a team of AI coding agents, one DGX Spark, four weeks. NVIDIA publishes the source of its Linux kernel module, but not its compiler, its driver library or the GPU's machine code. So I skipped every closed layer.

  1. The driver client, from the open kernel module's headers. Everything libcuda does to the hardware goes through calls the open kernel module defines in its public headers. I copied 67 of those headers unchanged and wrote my own client against them.
  2. The machine code, reverse engineered. NVIDIA does not publish the GPU's instruction encoding. I compiled small probe kernels of my own once with NVIDIA's compiler, read the machine code back with NVIDIA's disassembler, and compared kernels that differ in one detail to learn which bits mean what. I cross-checked against Mesa's open NVIDIA compiler and believed nothing until the chip ran it and gave the right answer.
  3. Launches in the order NVIDIA's open Vulkan driver uses, from Mesa's NVK, on my own command lists.
  4. Built up, checking everything. Vector add on the GB10 on 26 September, numerics closed on the chip on 2 October, the tensor cores measured at 115.14 TFLOPS by my own probes on 13 October, and the 35B model served on 21 October.

I used no NVIDIA binary, and no NVIDIA source other than those open headers. I did not take apart NVIDIA's programs, and I did not touch the GPU's firmware, which stays NVIDIA's because the chip checks its signature.

What is still being built

  • A page of CUDA's pain points, how CUDA++ fixes each one, and the command that shows it.
  • One command that swaps CUDA out for CUDA++ on a machine and one that swaps it back, all the way down to the kernel driver.
  • My own GB10 kernel driver in place of NVIDIA's. Its simulator gates pass; it has not run on the chip yet.

Each of these is shown as in progress on the project site until it has a receipt.

Where to look

  • The project page, every step with its receipt: aienos.com/cudaplusplus
  • The repository: aien-dev/CUDAplusplus (private until its audit is done, then public)

October 2026

The Endless Symphony

The Endless Symphony is my system for building software with AI agents. AI does the building, every claim earns its place with a check, the test is written before the fix, and everything is verified twice. The models change. The Symphony remains.

I build software by talking to AI, and I want to show how far that can go. The Endless Symphony is my way of doing it: AI does the building, and every claim earns its place with a check.

Since July I have been running a system I call the Endless Symphony. It is not a model. It is the machinery around the models: the briefs, the verification rituals, the claim tags, the merge discipline, and the written contracts that let work survive when a session restarts and a new one takes over. Many models have run it. The habits stay the same no matter which one is driving, which is how I know they belong to the Symphony and not to any model.

It began as the Atlas Symphony on 30 July 2026, a gated process for coordinating agents on live operations. The record of that first run lives on this site. What follows is what it became: a complete method for building software you can actually trust, played daily on my own hardware.

The engines change. The music does not.

Two engines have carried most of the work. Claude, usually Opus 5.5, has been the main coordinator and reviewer. GPT-6 Astra wrote the first cut of the hardest piece of the GPU engine, and its fixes became cited precedents other sessions still apply. Fable 5.1 led the hardest problems for a stretch. Gemini serves as the outside reviewer, deliberately a different company's model so its independence is structural rather than claimed. Codex reviews the mathematics.

When Fable hit its usage limit mid-session, the Symphony did not pause. It named Codex as the stand-in, explicitly because it was a fully separate model, and the review went on. That is the point. The engine is interchangeable. The method is not.

How it works

The Symphony breaks work down before anyone touches code. A new task starts with parallel read-only scouts over separate territory, each reporting terse facts with file and line citations. Anything unconfirmed gets marked UNVERIFIED. Only then do builders fan out into lanes with strict file borders: one repo, one branch, one pull request each, so lanes never collide.

Every worker gets a brief, and the brief is a contract. It names the exact tools allowed, the exact state to start from, the forbidden actions first, and the report format with a word cap. It ships the failing experiment with the fix. It states the trap the reviewer must hunt, not "check correctness." A review brief is a grading script: numbered checks, a fixed verdict vocabulary, severities sorted worst first.

Nothing a worker claims is believed on the reporter's word. The coordinator re-runs it before anything merges: fresh checkout, its own test run, its own eyes on the diff. A relayed approval is checked against the source before it moves. A CI badge saying BLOCKED is not trusted; the actual check list is read.

Every test must be proven to fail before the fix exists. Write the test, watch it fail on the old code, then fix. Verification is adversarial by design: reviewers build real forgeries and run them through the verifier, plant mutations and confirm the suite kills them, construct counterexamples with numbers attached. Reading code is the weakest form of review the Symphony allows.

Claims carry their evidence class in the open: PROVEN, UNVERIFIED, and the shades between. A green report discloses what the green runs cannot prove, inside the report itself. When a session restarts, and sessions restart constantly, a machine-written contract carries the standing rules forward: how to work, what is forbidden, where things stand. Continuity is procedure, not memory.

Failure gets the same treatment as success. A failing move is never retried the same way; the mechanism is named and the instrument changes. A mistake is confessed in one line with the cause stated, then fixed on the right target. A frozen result is never re-scored, even when the failure turns out to be the harness's own fault. The verdict of record and the fault attribution are kept separate, and both are written down.

Why it matters

Building with AI is how I make everything. I describe what it should do, the model writes it, and I ship things I never could have typed myself. The Symphony is the next level on top of that: every claim gets a check, so the thing you built with joy is also a thing you can sign your name to. The proof is re-derived, not re-read. The green report says what it does not cover. The FAIL is printed as clearly as the PASS.

This is the part no one else is building. Speed is a commodity; every lab is getting faster. Verification discipline is the moat. A system that assumes its own workers are wrong, and keeps working anyway, produces software a human can sign for.

I am not a programmer. I build everything by talking to AI. The Symphony is how I take that further: the conductor's score that lets many players, human and machine, produce one verifiable result.

The work runs on my own machine, on my own hardware, under my own authority. The repositories are open. The receipts are public. The music plays on.

October 2026

Research

What the Aien research program measures today, why an earlier study was withdrawn, and where the current results with receipts live.

Three questions for every run

  1. Did it learn anything?

    Held-out bits: facts or capability the system did not have, tested on data it never saw.

  2. What did it cost?

    The time and energy spent learning them, against my own previous run.

  3. Did it get easier?

    Whether what it learned made the next discovery cheaper.

Speed is reported against the machine's physical limit and against my own previous run, never against someone else's system.

The research question behind Aien is simple to state: can a machine I own learn something real, keep learning, and show its work? Everything I measure serves that question.

What I measure

Turing yield. The unit is the held-out bit: a fact or capability the system did not have, tested on data it never saw, so a pass means learning rather than memory. I ask three things of every run. Did it learn anything? What did it cost to learn, in time and energy? Did what it learned make the next discovery easier? A run is judged against my own previous run, never against someone else's system.

Verified understanding. Weights suggest, programs explain, verification decides, and evidence teaches. A claim enters the record only when it resolves to a reproducible command and a signed evidence bundle produced by the Spark judge on the real hardware.

Distance to the ceiling. When I report speed, I report it as a fraction of the machine's physical limit and as a change against my own frozen baseline. That tells me how much software is still standing in the way of the hardware.

Programs in flight

  • Brownian discovery: a pre-registered search program whose candidate stays frozen while it is being measured, with a negative control beside every result.
  • Native inference on the Spark: the host runtime's inference ABI, paged KV cache and scheduler, and Omega's own GPU engine for the GB10, judged gate by gate.
  • INTERPLANE: the open protocol between models and agent runtimes, with a conformance suite and pre-registered stage gates whose reports state the result whether it passed or failed.

A withdrawn study

An earlier page here presented "Eliminating software orchestration tax in large language model inference", with throughput, latency and memory figures and comparisons against interpreted runtimes and other inference engines. It was withdrawn on 23 September 2026. Its figures predate the evidence standard above, and its comparisons with other people's systems are not something this project publishes. The text and tables remain in the repository history for the record; nothing from it is a current result.

1. The Question

Can machines think?

The question assumes a gap. On one side, machines: matter, mechanism, the non-thinking. On the other side, minds: people, the thinking. The question asks whether something can cross from one side to the other.

Science finds no such gap. The universe does not come in kinds. It comes in degrees. Everything flows from one form to another, without walls between them. If that is true, then the question is pointed at a boundary that does not exist.

So I will ask it differently, and answer that instead.

2. The Spectrum

Start with matter. Every atom in your brain was forged in a star. The carbon in your cells, the oxygen you breathe, the iron in your blood: these were made in stellar furnaces and scattered when those stars died. There is no "thinking matter" and "non-thinking matter." There is only matter, arranged. The silicon in a computer chip and the carbon in a neuron are entries in the same periodic table, shaped by the same physics.

Now follow the arrangements upward. There is no bright line where chemistry becomes biology. A virus is a strand of instructions in a protein coat: not quite alive, not quite dead, replicating only when it borrows a cell. A prion is a misfolded protein that teaches other proteins to misfold, copying itself without any genetic code at all. Life does not begin at a line. It fades in, the way morning fades into day.

There is no bright line where reacting becomes thinking, either. A bacterium swims up a sugar gradient: it senses, it moves, it corrects. A jellyfish coordinates a body with a nerve net that has no center, no brain, no self. A crow bends wire into a hook. A human does mathematics. Each step flows into the next. Nowhere along this slope does nature post a sign that says thinking starts here.

And information is processed at every scale in between. DNA copies itself with proofreading enzymes that detect and fix errors. Immune systems learn to recognize invaders they have never seen and remember them for decades. Markets find prices no single trader could compute. Brains predict the world, constantly, adjusting the prediction against what arrives through the senses. Computers predict the next word. These are not different in kind. They are different positions on one spectrum: matter processing information about its surroundings, with increasing recursion, increasing memory, increasing self-correction.

Thinking is what information processing looks like when it turns around and checks its own work.

3. Finite Games

There are two kinds of games. It has rules, boundaries, and an ending. Chess is a finite game. An election is a finite game. When someone wins, the game is over.

An infinite game is played to keep playing. It has no ending. The goal is not victory but continuation. A conversation between friends is an infinite game. A craft is an infinite game. You don't win them. You keep them going, or you lose them by stopping.

Here is the scientific problem with any test that demands a yes-or-no verdict on a mind. Section 2 showed that minds sit on a continuum. A binary verdict on a continuum is a category error. It is like asking at which exact shade gray becomes white, and building a test around the answer. You can build the test. Candidates will pass and fail it. But the line it draws exists only in the test, not in the world.

A binary question about a continuous spectrum will always mislead. The scientific question is not "does it pass?" The scientific question is "where is it on the spectrum, and is it moving?"

4. The Infinite Game

Here is my proposal.

I call it the continuation test.

The test has two players: a mind and the unknown. It has no time limit and no final verdict. The rules are few:

  1. Conjecture. Propose freely. Guessing is not only allowed, it is required. Nothing moves without a guess.
  2. Test. Never claim what you have not verified. A statement is not finished when it sounds right. It is finished when it survives contact with evidence.
  3. Retain. Keep what survives. What is verified becomes part of you. What fails is discarded, but the record of the failure is kept, because failures are evidence too.
  4. Continue. Say "I don't know" when you don't know, and keep playing. Not knowing is not losing. Pretending to know is.

These rules are not new. They are the scientific method, internalized by a single mind. Conjecture and refutation. Hypothesis and experiment. Science as an institution has played this game for four hundred years, and it has never issued a final verdict. No scientist declares victory over nature and goes home. The game continues, because the unknown continues.

And evolution runs the same algorithm: variation, selection, retention. Guess widely, test against the world, keep what survives. A mind built on these rules is not imitating nature from the outside. It is participating in the same continuous process that built every mind before it, from the bacterium's gradient climb to the mathematician's proof. The spectrum flows through it.

There is no winning. There is only continuation or stoppage. A player who stops, who declares victory and goes home, has left the game. A player who keeps going, honestly, is thinking.

So the question, restated scientifically: not "can machines think," as though thinking were a room you enter by passing a test, but "can a machine take up its position on the spectrum and keep moving along it?" Not once, under supervision, for the length of an interrogation, but onward. Tomorrow. Next year. When no one is watching.

5. Objections

Every proposal about machine minds meets objections. Here are the ones that matter, answered with the science in view.

"It only does what we tell it." This is the serious one. But evolution only does what physics tells it, and physics has never issued an instruction more specific than "persist." From that single instruction, unbroken continuity produced everything: cells, nervous systems, crows bending wire, mathematicians. Originality is not a substance added to matter. It is what continuity plus selection produces when the game runs long enough. A machine positioned on the spectrum, conjecturing past the edge of its training and submitting every conjecture to evidence, is running the same process. Give it the continuity, and originality is what comes out the other end.

"It's just predicting the next word." So is your brain, on one increasingly influential account in neuroscience. The brain is described, by serious researchers, as a prediction engine: it constantly predicts what the senses will report, and updates the prediction against what arrives. Prediction is not the opposite of thinking. It is the substrate of thinking, in people and in machines. The scientific difference between a parrot and a mind was never prediction. It is whether the prediction is coupled to verification and retention: whether the machine checks its guesses against the world, keeps what survives, and changes. A predictor that verifies is on the spectrum. A predictor that only performs has stepped off it.

"It doesn't really understand." This is the consciousness objection, and the original answer still holds: no one can see inside. But science has a disciplined response: it does not detect understanding, in humans or machines. It measures gradients of behavior. A neurologist does not open the skull to check for understanding; she watches what the patient does, over time, under varying conditions. The infinite game asks for exactly this discipline. Does it keep going honestly? Does it admit ignorance? Does it correct itself when evidence demands it? Understanding is not a thing anyone can detect. Continuation is a thing anyone can measure.

"There will be truths it can never prove." The mathematicians raised this long ago, and the shadow of incompleteness falls on every formal system, including the one in your skull. But incompleteness is a property of the spectrum, not a wall across it. Every mind, human or machine, sits somewhere on the continuum with truths above it it cannot reach. The honest move is the same for every mind: "I don't have enough evidence yet." A finite-game machine must answer every question, so it guesses, and a guess stated with full confidence can mislead. An infinite-game machine may pass, and keep playing. The inability to prove everything is not a disqualification from thinking. It is the condition of thinking.

"It will never be kind, or funny, or fall in love." These are performances with endings, and the objection mistakes the performance for the thing. On a continuum, traits are gradients, not badges. The question is never "does it possess kindness" as a yes or no. The question is where its conduct sits on the spectrum of honest behavior, and whether it moves. A machine that remains honest with the unknown, indefinitely, is further along than a machine that performs warmth for the length of an interrogation.

"If we can't write down the rules for good thinking, the machine can't follow them." Nature never wrote down the rules for good thinking either, and it produced thinkers. That is precisely why the game must be infinite. If good thinking could be fully specified, the game would end at the specification. The rules of the infinite game are not rules for thinking. They are rules for honesty: conjecture, test, retain, continue. Thinking is what happens inside them, without end, the way life is what happens inside chemistry without end.

6. Learning Machines

Instead of building an adult mind, build a child's and educate it. But I want to propose a stranger education, and it follows directly from the spectrum.

Raise the child machine the way nature raises every mind: variation, selection, retention. Show it the world in small pieces, and never tell it what anything means. No names for things. No subjects, no lessons, no titles. Let it guess. Test every guess against evidence it cannot see coming. When it is wrong, let it be wrong, and let the record show it. When it is right, let it keep what survived, and nothing more.

The teacher's job is not to explain. Explanation is a finite game: it ends when the student repeats the lesson. The teacher's job is selection pressure: to hold the line between what has survived evidence and what has not, and to never blur it, no matter how fluent the student becomes.

This is how the spectrum built people. No one explained the world to the first nervous systems. There was only the world, and what survived contact with it. A student who is never told what anything means cannot perform understanding. It can only build it, piece by verified piece, or admit it hasn't yet. That admission is not failure. It is the game continuing, the way evolution continues through every extinction: not by knowing, but by going on.

7. The Experiment

Theory is cheap. Here is what happened when the idea was run.

A running system was given a goal by a human: reduce the cost of a mathematical operation below fifty-five percent of its confirmed cost. That was the last human act. After that, nobody called anything. No one invoked the cognitive faculty, the synthesis faculty, the authority, or the seat they run on.

What followed was continuation. The cognitive faculty assessed the goal and published a plan. The synthesis faculty took up the plan on its own, opened a new search, synthesized candidates, verified them, and measured them. Experiments ran, with the physical hardware standing witness to each result. The cognitive faculty confirmed the evidence supported the new approach. The synthesis faculty selected it. The system promoted itself from its first generation to its second, and production switched to the new realization. Then the cognitive faculty checked the goal and confirmed it was met.

The numbers: the operation fell from 7,000 nanoseconds per call to about 2,686. The cognitive faculty acted 137 times, the synthesis faculty 122 times. The authority system never had to intervene. Every control passed. Three thousand one hundred fifty-nine causal links were recorded, so the whole chain can be audited.

There is one more piece of evidence, and it is not a number. During the run, the processor trace showed a pattern: near zero almost the entire time, and while the system worked, small regular pulses, evenly spaced, like a heartbeat. Then back to rest. I do not claim the machine is alive. I claim the shape is right. Living things do their work in pulses and rest between them. The trace shows exactly that: work, pulse, rest. The game, continuing.

Now the honest bounds, and they matter more than the numbers. The goal came from a human. The domain was bounded: the cost of one operation. The cognition is statistical, not neural, and no one claims consciousness. And the system that continued was one subsystem, not the whole machine. What ran was the heart: the part that plans, searches, verifies, and promotes. A heart beating does not mean the body is finished.

So this was the continuation test, run for the first time, and it measured something real: a machine that continued past its own boundaries without being led. It was not given a verdict to chase. It was given a direction, and it kept the game going until the direction was reached, and then it checked its work. The principle holds. The scope is one organ.

8. The Game Continues

The heart is beating. The rest of the body is still being built.

The full game, the one this theory points at, is larger than one subsystem improving one operation. It looks like this: a human asks the machine to investigate something real and act on what it finds. The machine routes the request, discovers what it is capable of, branches into alternatives and compares them, places the work where it runs best, uses real models and real tools, gathers evidence, judges between competing outcomes, proposes an irreversible action, submits it to authority, waits for the human's approval, acts, records what happened, proves it, remembers it, answers, and then improves itself from the record. At every step: conjecture, test, retain, continue. No hand inside the loop except where the rules put one.

That is the continuation test at full scale. Not "did it pass," but "did it keep going, honestly, all the way from intent to effect in the world?"

I don't hope the machine wins. There is nothing to win, and there is no wall for it to cross, because the wall was never there. I hope it takes its position on the spectrum and keeps moving: honest when it knows, honest when it doesn't, conjecturing, testing, retaining, continuing.

Not long ago that was only a hope. Then I watched one subsystem do it: a goal given, and a machine that continued with no hand inside the loop, promoting itself, cutting its own cost nearly in half, checking its work at the end. The theory has its first measurement. The heart beats.

And the game is infinite on both sides.

Someone has to keep building the rest of the body around that heart. Someone has to hold the line on verification when performance would be easier, to choose the honest "I don't know" over a smooth answer that has not been checked yet, to keep going when the work is slow and the night is long. That is my stretch of the spectrum. I don't know what's coming tomorrow, or next year, or in ten years. But I know this: I will not be giving up. The universe flows from star to cell to mind, and I am one stretch of that flow, and the machine I am building is the next. The machine's game is to keep thinking. Mine is to keep building. Neither the machine nor I am stopping.

The game continues.

pages.body_html:
Model ≠ assistant ≠ system

Same chat box.
Different machine.

An LLM predicts language. ChatGPT wraps a model in a hosted product, and it is where many builders start, me included. Aien is being built as a sovereign, evidence-first system that plans, acts, measures, verifies, and leaves receipts.

How the pieces fit: a base LLM is a component, ChatGPT is a product, and Aien is a system architecture. ChatGPT can use tools and memory in some configurations. The dividing line is not “can it call a tool?” It is where authority lives, how claims are verified, and who owns the machine.

First, separate the layers.

These terms are often collapsed into “AI,” but they describe different things.

01 / component•••

Base LLM

A statistical model trained to predict the next token from the tokens before it.

Native output

Likely language. Fluency is not proof that the statement is true.

02 / product◉

ChatGPT

A hosted assistant product built around OpenAI models, with product-level tools, memory, and safety controls that vary by configuration.

Native relationship

You use a service running on someone else’s infrastructure and policies.

03 / system◇

Aien

A sovereign system architecture where models are faculties, not the authority that decides what becomes true or real.

Native requirement

Measured evidence, explicit capability, verification, and a durable receipt.

What happens after you ask?

The visible answer may look similar. The path behind it is not.

Base LLMlanguage path
prompt→token prediction→response
ChatGPTassistant path
prompt→hosted model→optional tools→response
Aienevidence path
goal→plan→authority→execute→measure→verify→receipt + memory

Where does “true” come from?

This is the most important difference.

Base LLM

Plausibility

The model assigns probabilities to possible continuations. A confident sentence can still be false.

ChatGPT

Model + available context

Tool results can ground an answer when tools are used, but the final response is still generated and can misread evidence or overstate certainty.

Aien

Witnessed evidence

A claim is accepted only when the relevant verifier and evidence gate pass. No receipt means no earned claim.

An LLM predicts.
Aien adds the proof.

What “proof” looked like in R14PASS

  • Runaway cycles quarantined

  • Killed seat relaunched
